stem: How does a magnetic hard disk record a binary digit?

options.content: As a magnetised area of the platter surface
options.rationale: Correct: the head magnetises a tiny area in one of two directions.

options.content: As a pit or a land in a spiral track
options.rationale: That describes an optical disc.

options.content: As charge trapped on a floating gate in a cell
options.rationale: That describes flash memory in an SSD.

options.content: As a voltage held by a capacitor that is refreshed
options.rationale: That describes DRAM, which is primary memory.

explanation: A hard disk stores bits as the direction of magnetism in tiny areas of a coated platter.

stem: Which feature of a solid-state drive makes it better than a hard disk when it is carried around on a bumpy road?

options.content: It has no moving parts that can be damaged
options.rationale: Correct: there are no platters or heads to be knocked.

options.content: It has a larger capacity for the same price
options.rationale: Capacity per price is usually in favour of the hard disk.

options.content: It uses a laser to read the data quickly
options.rationale: Lasers are used in optical drives, not SSDs.

options.content: It stores data in magnetised tracks that cannot move
options.rationale: SSDs do not use magnetism.

explanation: An SSD has no spinning platters or moving heads, so a knock is much less likely to damage it.

stem: A drive shines a laser at a disc and a sensor measures how much light is reflected. What is being read?

options.content: The direction of magnetism on the platter
options.rationale: A magnetic head senses magnetism; a laser does not.

options.content: The charge on a floating gate
options.rationale: Flash cells are read electrically, not with light.

options.content: The sector number under a read-write head
options.rationale: Sector addressing is part of a hard disk, which uses no laser.

options.content: The pits and lands on the track
options.rationale: Correct: lands reflect strongly and pits scatter the light.

explanation: Optical storage reads the difference in reflection between pits and lands.

stem: A surveyor in Hwange must keep a copy of a large map database in the office safe, away from the laptop she uses in the field. Which is the most suitable backup device?

options.content: A second partition on the laptop's own drive
options.rationale: A copy on the same drive is lost if that drive fails or is stolen.

options.content: The laptop's RAM
options.rationale: RAM loses its data when the power is off and is not a backup.

options.content: An external hard disk
options.rationale: Correct: large capacity, low cost per GiB and easily stored elsewhere.

options.content: A small memory card in the laptop's slot
options.rationale: The card stays with the laptop and may be too small for a large database.

explanation: A backup should be on a different device and in a different place, with enough capacity for the data.
hints: A backup must survive the loss of the laptop.

stem: What does the term rotational latency mean for a hard disk?

options.content: The time taken for the arm to move to the correct track on the platter
options.rationale: That is the seek time.

options.content: The time taken to copy the data to main memory
options.rationale: That is the transfer time.

options.content: The wait for the required sector to turn under the head
options.rationale: Correct: it is the delay caused by the spinning of the platter.

options.content: The number of times the platter is rewritten each year
options.rationale: Rewrite limits concern flash memory, not latency.

explanation: Access time is seek time (moving the arm) plus rotational latency (waiting for the sector) plus transfer time.
hints: The latency is caused by the platter spinning, not by the arm.

stem: Why do the controllers of solid-state drives use wear levelling?

options.content: To keep the platters spinning at an even speed
options.rationale: SSDs have no platters.

options.content: To make the laser focus on the correct track
options.rationale: SSDs have no laser.

options.content: To refresh the capacitors in each cell every few milliseconds
options.rationale: Refreshing is needed for DRAM, not for flash.

options.content: To spread writes so that no block is erased too often
options.rationale: Correct: each flash block survives a limited number of erase cycles.

explanation: Because flash cells wear out after many erase cycles, the controller spreads the writes evenly across all blocks.
hints: What limits the life of a flash cell?

stem: A school wants to store 4 TiB of old exam papers that will rarely be read, as cheaply as possible, and does not need fast access. Which statement gives the best justification for a hard disk rather than an SSD?

options.content: It has no moving parts, so it is the most durable option
options.rationale: Moving parts are a weakness of a hard disk.

options.content: It gives more storage for a lower cost per GiB
options.rationale: Correct: capacity and cost matter more than speed here.

options.content: It uses less power than any SSD in all situations
options.rationale: SSDs usually use less power.

options.content: It reads data faster because it needs no seek
options.rationale: Hard disks must seek, so they are generally slower.

explanation: For large, rarely used archives, low cost per GiB is the deciding factor, and the slower access does not matter.
hints: Which two features matter most in this scenario?

stem: On an optical disc, the pits reflect more light back to the sensor than the lands do.
explanation: False. Lands are flat and reflect the light strongly; pits scatter it, so less light reaches the sensor.

stem: A solid-state drive has no read-write head.
explanation: True. An SSD reads and writes through electronic circuits connected to its flash cells; heads belong to hard disks.

stem: Match each storage device to the way in which it holds a bit.

right.content: Pit or land on a spiral track
Pit read by a blue-violet laser
Charge trapped on a floating gate

explanation: Magnetism, trapped charge and physical pits are the three methods; Blu-ray uses a shorter wavelength laser than a DVD.

stem: Complete the description of a hard disk.

payload.template: Data is stored on spinning {{blank:a}} divided into tracks and {{blank:b}}. A {{blank:c}} on a moving arm magnetises and senses the surface.

explanation: A hard disk has platters divided into tracks and sectors, and a read-write head on an arm.

stem: A hard disk spins at 6000 revolutions per minute. Calculate the average rotational latency in milliseconds, assuming the sector is on average half a turn away.
explanation: One revolution takes 10 ms, so the average wait is 5 ms.
workedSolution:
1. One revolution = 60 ÷ 6000 = 0.01 s = 10 ms.
2. Average latency = half a revolution = 5 ms.

stem: The disk in the previous question has an average seek time of 10 ms. Calculate its average access time, ignoring the transfer time.
explanation: Access time = 10 ms + 5 ms = 15 ms.
workedSolution:
1. Average latency = 5 ms (half of 10 ms).
2. Access time = seek + latency = 10 + 5 = 15 ms.
hints: Access time = seek time + rotational latency.

stem: A backup copies 2 GiB of files to an external drive at a steady 128 MiB per second. How many seconds does the copy take?
explanation: 2048 MiB ÷ 128 MiB per second = 16 s.
hints: Convert 2 GiB to MiB first (1 GiB = 1024 MiB).

stem: A flash memory chip stores 1 GiB. Each cell holds 2 bits. How many cells does the chip contain?
explanation: 2^33 bits at 2 bits per cell gives 2^32 = 4 294 967 296 cells.
hints: Bits = bytes × 8; each cell holds 2 bits.

stem: Describe how data is read from an optical disc. [4]

points.description: Data is stored on a spiral track of pits and lands
A laser shines onto the track as the disc spins
Lands reflect the light strongly and pits scatter it
A sensor detects the reflected light and the changes are interpreted as the binary data

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The disc has a spiral track of pits and lands. As it spins, a laser is shone onto the track. Lands reflect the light and pits scatter it, and a sensor reads the changes in reflected light as binary data.

explanation: One mark for each stage.
hints: Four points: spiral track, laser, reflection, interpretation.

stem: Explain why a solid-state drive is more suitable than a hard disk for a rugged handheld tablet used on farms. [3]

points.description: No moving parts, so it survives knocks and vibration
Uses less power, so the battery lasts longer
Faster access, so programs and files open quickly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An SSD has no moving parts so knocks do not damage it, it uses less power so the battery lasts longer, and it gives faster access to data.

explanation: Durability, power use and speed are the expected advantages.
hints: Link each reason to a handheld device, such as a rugged tablet.

stem: A secondary school in Kariba keeps the term's examination marks on one office computer. Design a backup plan. [4]

points.description: Copy the data to a different device, such as an external hard disk or memory card
Keep the copy in a different place (for example a locked cabinet in another building)
Back up regularly (for example every evening or after each marks entry session)
Check occasionally that the backup can be restored

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Copy the marks every evening to an external hard disk. Keep the disk in a locked cabinet in a different building so that fire or theft in the office cannot destroy both copies. Test that the files can be restored once a term.

explanation: Credit a different device, a different place, regularity and testing.
hints: Where is the copy kept, on what, how often?

stem: A hospital in Mutare compares two drives for storing scanned patient records. Drive X is a hard disk spinning at 7200 rpm with an average seek time of 8 ms. Drive Y is a solid-state drive.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the time for one revolution of drive X, in milliseconds, to 2 decimal places.
parts.workedSolution:
1. 7200 rpm = 7200 revolutions in 60 s.
2. One revolution = 60 ÷ 7200 s = 0.008333 s = 8.33 ms.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the average access time of drive X, in milliseconds, to 2 decimal places. Ignore the transfer time.
parts.explanation: Seek 8 ms plus average latency 4.17 ms gives 12.17 ms.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Average latency = 8.33 ÷ 2 = 4.17 ms.
2. Access time = 8 + 4.17 = 12.17 ms.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give two reasons why drive Y has a shorter access time than drive X.

points.description: It has no seek time because there is no arm to move
It has no rotational latency because nothing has to spin to the data

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: There is no arm to move and no platter to wait for, so data is found almost immediately.

parts.explanation: Both seek time and rotational latency are removed.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The hospital stores 30 TiB of scans that are seldom opened. State which drive type it should buy and justify the choice.

points.description: Hard disk
Lower cost per GiB / larger capacity for the money, and speed is not critical

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A hard disk, because it stores very large amounts at a lower cost per GiB and fast access is not needed for rarely opened files.

parts.explanation: Cost and capacity decide for an archive.

explanation: Latency is half of 8.33 ms; access time adds the seek time; an SSD has neither delay; a hard disk is cheaper per GiB for an archive.
hints: Compare the two drives using the stated feature.

stem: A school computer laboratory is fitted with solid-state drives that use flash memory.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is held on the floating gate of a flash cell?

options.content: A magnetic pole
options.rationale: Magnetism is used in hard disks.

options.content: Trapped electrons
options.rationale: Correct: the trapped charge represents the stored bit.

options.content: A pit or land
options.rationale: These are on optical discs.

options.content: A capacitor charge that is refreshed
options.rationale: DRAM needs refreshing; flash does not.

parts.explanation: Electrons trapped on the floating gate keep their charge when the power is off.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why each block of flash memory can only be erased a limited number of times and what the controller does about it.

points.description: Each erase cycle gradually damages the insulating layer so the cell wears out
The controller uses wear levelling to spread writes evenly over all blocks

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Every erase damages the insulating layer a little, so cells eventually fail. Wear levelling spreads writes across all blocks.

parts.explanation: Cause and remedy for one mark each.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State three advantages of SSDs over hard disks for the laboratory.

points.description: Faster access to files
Silent / no moving parts so more robust
Lower power consumption

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: They are faster, silent and robust with no moving parts, and they use less power.

explanation: Flash holds trapped electrons on floating gates, wears out after many erases, and gives speed, silence and durability.
hints: Think about what is trapped in the floating gate.
